You wake up in a body that isn’t yours.

The face in the washbasin is unfamiliar. Your last life is still there, clear enough to remember the small things. A different ceiling hangs above the bed. Outside the window, a cart wheel bumps over a stone and somebody tells its driver to slow down.

A woman takes a bowl from the stove. There is sand beneath the chair beside you. Painted lamp covers hang above a table crowded with brushes.

“We found you on the shore,” she says. “Kenta ran for me. You’ve been here since dawn.”

At the open door, a young man with a turquoise shirt and muddy boots shifts a basket against his hip.

“I’ll tell Haruho I’ll be late,” he says. Then, to her, “Actually late. I mean it this time.”

“Might make a useful change.”

He gives a small, chastened grin and waits by the door. The woman brings the broth within reach. Her hands smell faintly of lamp oil and orange peel.

“Mihana,” she says, touching her own chest. “This is Brookmeadow. When you feel up to it, tell me what to call you.”

Red pennants snap above Phoenix Wing’s gate. Older students stream past with practice bags and breakfast rolls; the newcomers slow at every doorway, unwilling to be the first to admit they have lost the signs. Behind the training wall, a whistle cuts through the clack of wooden weapons.

At the Main Hall desk, a clerk checks the new arrival against the admitted list and hands over a folded timetable. A red line beneath the morning subjects marks an afternoon preparation period. At the bottom, in heavier ink: FIRST DEFENSIVE PRACTICAL — PARTNER WORK.

Hinae Komori is still looking at that line when Nemu Usami leans over her shoulder.

“At least they’re telling us in advance,” Hinae says. “I’d like someone to tell me what they mean by ‘under pressure.’”

“Probably not a comfortable chair,” Nemu replies. Her rabbit ears twitch toward the training wall. “I intend to raise an objection.”

Kokona Hanamori arrives with a small bag of sweets and offers one to Hinae. Nemu reaches for it first. “I’m arranging a preparation table,” Kokona says. “If you’re going to sleep through it, at least don’t take the last one.”

Riko Umezawa pauses on her way to a returning-year session. “You’re spending an entire afternoon on the first practice?”

“Some of us need the practice,” Hinae says.

“And some of us need the sweets,” Nemu adds. Riko laughs, checks her own room number and hurries on before anyone can ask how much preparation she has done.

The welcome bell gathers the first-years into the hall. Kōhei Sanada waits for the last bench to stop scraping before he speaks.

“You will study Magic Theory, Magical Combat, and Potions and Alchemy. Attend your scheduled lessons. Prepare the work we assign. Talent excuses neither absence nor putting another person in danger.”

He lays one hand on the lectern.

“Your first practical is about protecting someone. You may discover that keeping a partner safe is less flattering than winning a duel. Learn the difference. Your instructors will tell you what needs improving, and you will have a chance to improve it.”

Outside the east doors, Takeru Akabane is fastening a dueling-club notice to the board. The second-year catches a falling tack before it reaches the floor. “Open practice after the preparation block,” he tells the passing group. “Watch, try a drill, see whether you like it. You don’t have to join to show up.”

The headmaster returns toward Faculty Offices while the first-years find the Lecture Hall. Haruki Saitō has placed a wooden screen, a chalk line and a padded target near the front. He checks the stopper on his travel mug before lifting the screen far enough to reveal a gap at its base.

“A shield can be quite sound,” he says, “and still leave somebody unprotected. Start with what you can observe. What would you check before trusting this position?”

Hinae crouches far enough to examine the gap without crossing the chalk. “Nemu, can you see the target from your side?”

Nemu studies the distance to the nearest bench. “I can supervise.”

The screen is still raised. Several students move for a better view; others are already disagreeing about the safest place to stand. There is room to inspect, speak or join the exercise.

A box of brass fittings rattles past Gryffin Tail’s entrance on a handcart. Two returning students argue over whether the noise is normal. Neither slows down. Blue banners move above the courtyard, and the first-years cluster near the Main Hall desk with the concentrated expressions of people trying to look at home.

The clerk hands the new arrival a timetable. Morning subjects fill the first block; a preparation session follows later in the day. A separate notice names the first demonstration: A CLAIM WORTH TESTING.

Nahlah Qamar has caught a beetle on the back of her hand. Her turquoise eyes follow its legs as it negotiates a seam in her cuff.

“It keeps choosing the darker edge,” she says. “Or perhaps that’s simply where I keep tilting my hand. I haven’t decided.”

Tatsuo Nagase peers over. “If we’re studying insects, can the question be whether they eat the grain in my lunch?”

“You would need to let it near your lunch.”

He considers the cost and steps back.

Norio Shibata’s welcome begins without a grand flourish. He names Magic Theory, Magical Engineering and Magical Arts, then lifts one of the demonstration notices.

“You are here to become capable of finding things out. An impressive explanation is useful only if it survives contact with the thing explained. Bring a question you can actually test. Tell us what happened, including the part you hoped would go differently.”

He makes the attendance and preparation requirements plain. Students who struggle will receive specific work to improve; the school will not accept invented results in place of that work.

At the corridor board, Satoru Kanda is arranging a small display for a second-year study circle. His diagram is immaculate. The little rotor beneath it refuses to turn. Renji Hanabusa has already written an enthusiastic description of the finished demonstration.

“That is a loose contact,” Satoru says before anyone asks.

“Then the description is accurate in principle,” Renji replies.

Mitsuki Amano sets her crystal sphere beyond the rotor’s reach. “If either of you knocks this off the stand, your next experiment can be putting it back together.” They are returning second-years, and their own work is clearly not finished. The open-session notice invites first-years to bring questions after their preparation block.

The headmaster heads back to Faculty Offices. Inside the Lecture Hall, Kei Aoki has set two apparently identical glass vessels on the desk. A narrow streamer moves beside one and hangs motionless beside the other.

“You can ask to inspect them,” Kei tells the room. “You can propose a test. You cannot tell me you know what is inside because you prefer one explanation.”

Nahlah compares the vessels from the edge of her table. Tatsuo looks at the streamer, then tries to see beneath the desk without leaving his place.

“I’d like to know whether we’re allowed to touch the table.”

Two students behind them propose different explanations at once. Kei asks which observation would distinguish them. The vessels remain available for a closer look.

Yellow-and-gold banners hang over Dragon Hoard’s orderly entrance. Beyond the first court, porters are checking sealed equipment cases against a list. A group of older students waits beside them, trying to appear less interested in the names on the expedition notice than they plainly are.

The registrar finds the new arrival’s name and supplies a first-year timetable. Alongside the required morning subjects is a preparation block for a supervised field-readiness exercise. No distant destination is promised. The notice says that instructors will remember how students handle an uncertain find.

Chiyo Tsukikage reads the heading with grave satisfaction.

“At last. The first seal upon the path of forbidden—”

“It says training object,” Suzune Mikazuki interrupts. She has turned her broad shield to avoid blocking the desk. “I’d like to see the handling instructions before anybody breaks a seal.”

Yūji Nishimura checks the two papers in his own hands. “If one of you needs someone to carry the notes, I can do that. Or something more useful. Either.”

The first-years are called into the welcome. Miyu Asahina lets her eyes travel over their untidy row before she begins.

“Magic Theory, Spellcraft and Magical Creatures form your core timetable. You will prepare for them. Our expeditions are not prizes for whoever reaches an object first. Other people must be able to trust your observations, your hands and your account of what happened.”

She gestures toward the cases beyond the court.

“There are opportunities here worth working for. There are also people prepared to mistake attention for achievement. Learn to distinguish them in yourselves.”

In the corridor afterward, Ryūka Marufuji is studying the expedition notice while Ema Tsunoda sorts colored sample labels beside her. Both are second-years with their own preparations to finish.

“Those could have been plain,” Ryūka says.

“And someone could have mixed them up in bad light,” Ema replies, holding the labels against each other. “Are you helping me test them, or giving another opinion?”

Ryūka takes a pair with a small, sharp smile. “Apparently both.”

A nearby creature-observation group has advertised an open session after preparation; its demonstration remains optional. Miyu returns to Faculty Offices, and the first-years reach Noriaki Takatsuki’s Lecture Hall.

On the front table sits a closed training case beside a sketch of what it supposedly contains. The fastening on the actual case faces a different way.

“Before we discuss the spell,” Noriaki says, “tell me what you would establish before opening this.”

Chiyo has already noticed the mismatch and is arguing that it must be deliberate. Suzune wants to know how the case was transported. Yūji begins comparing the sketch with the fastening. Their discussion leaves several ways for another student to contribute—or challenge the premise.

Violet cloth stirs above Hydra Head’s court. Someone is moving planters away from a doorway while a second student insists that the sign saying KEEP CLEAR refers to the other doorway. The queue of new arrivals divides around them and reforms at the Main Hall desk.

The clerk supplies a timetable and a short preparation notice. Morning classes are required. An afternoon work session precedes the first civic exercise: a shared garden and practice space must serve several groups with different needs.

Gaku Inukai, wearing a second-year helper’s ribbon, is offering to organize the new students’ preparation groups.

“One list, everything settled. Very efficient.”

Bunta Ushijima holds the list upside down. “Do they know what you’ve promised them?”

“They will when we have enough people.”

Near the planters, Homura Hibino lowers a rolled diagram and examines the practice-space notice. “If nobody uses the east corner, it would be ideal for a small demonstration.”

“How small?” Bunta asks.

“That depends on whether they give me the east corner.”

Asuka Tsurugi, a third-year on her way to practice, stops to point out that the east corner is beside the dueling approach. Fourth-year Tamaki Kiryū checks the bookings rather than joining the argument.

“You can have the demonstration after the practice ends,” Tamaki says. “If the smoke clears before my group arrives.”

“There doesn’t have to be smoke,” Homura objects, with insufficient conviction. None of them has abandoned their own morning for the newcomers.

The welcome bell intervenes. The older helpers step aside as the first-years gather before Kiyoko Fujinami. She names Magic Theory, Enchantment and Herbology and makes the timetable’s obligations clear.

“People will ask what your education is worth when something needs to work,” she says. “An agreement is not useful because it sounds gracious. Someone must be able to carry it out. You will prepare your proposals, listen to objections, and learn what your promises cost other people.”

She does not promise an answer that satisfies everyone. Students will receive feedback, and work that fails can be revised. Ignoring the people affected by it is another matter.

In the corridor, a notice invites newcomers to an open performance-and-garden gathering after the preparation block. There are names beside the jobs that still need doing, rather than a demand to join. Kiyoko returns to Faculty Offices while Kana Fujimoto receives the first-years in the Lecture Hall.

Kana has set a small planted tray beside a copper warming charm. The tray’s owner wants the roots kept cool; another group needs the warm space for its work. A sketch of the shared bench lies between them.

“Before offering a compromise,” Kana says, “what would you need to know?”

Gaku pauses beside the door and revises his list. Bunta leans over to check whether the promised groups actually exist.

Several first-years begin inspecting the planted tray while another asks how long the charm must run. There is no agreed proposal yet, and no assigned spokesperson.

Morning sun falls in green and honey-colored pieces across the guildhall tiles. At the appraisal bench beyond the counter, Karia Morino has propped her scythe safely clear of the aisle. Her coat is dusty, Renpei Sugita’s field map has dried into a curl, and Tetsuya Kanamori is examining a torn fastening with deep personal disapproval.

“The delivery arrived,” Renpei says. “We got everyone across.”

“After the cart stopped,” Karia replies, “you tried to lift it before checking what it was caught on.”

“I was trying to help.”

“You did help. After you stopped lifting it.”

Tetsuya holds the fastening up to the light. “And next time this comes to me before it tears. I charge less for a thing that is still one thing.”

Renpei begins defending the knot on his map case instead. Karia laughs, asks where he put their return note and starts checking her own pockets. Their difficult journey is over; settling its small consequences plainly is not.

At the counter, a young woman in a brick-red waistcoat is drawing something with far too many legs in the corner of her own scrap paper. Her peach-colored ponytails shift as she looks up, blue eyes bright.

“Welcome. New registration, looking for work, or here to explain why the parcel is making that noise?”

Komugi Hanabishi slides the scrap beneath a ledger with a completely unconvincing air of innocence.

“If you’re applying, we’ll start with the licensure assessment. You can use what you actually know—blade, bow, magic, whatever your method is. If you already have a genuine badge, show me and we can look at the board.”

Behind her, marked drawers hold records. Across the hall, bronze, silver, gold and pale platinum tabs divide the notices. A kettle clicks softly near the communal tables; beyond a rear doorway, a practice target swings and settles.

“And when you do take a job, find out who is depending on it,” Komugi adds. “If the plan stops working, tell us. Someone can arrange help for a late delivery. They can’t arrange much for a person who simply disappears.”

She rests her pen against the open ledger.

“So. What brings you to our counter?”

The receiving room smells of clean wood and yesterday's rain. Beyond an open screen, someone in the practice court is making the same mistake for the fourth time. The answering correction is considerably louder than the strike.

Ayame Kagetsuna stands beside a low map table, one sleeve tied back, arguing with a courier about a cart.

“It has two wheels. I am reasonably sure the road has room for both.”

“The porter says the load is ceremonial.”

“Then it can be ceremonially moved six inches to the left.”

The courier leaves with the air of a man who intends to quote that exactly. Ayame turns toward you. Her amber eyes travel to the mud by the threshold and then back to your face.

“Good. You're here. We have a short delivery waiting at the south yard. It needs an escort who can solve an argument without making it a duel.”

She folds the corner of the map clear. A bright cord marks the maintained road, ending at a bridge repair. Behind her, a servant carries a tray past two retainers pretending not to listen.

“Ask what is being carried. Ask who owns it. And if the answer is ‘because my cousin said so,’ ask another question.”

Her mouth twitches.

“If you have questions about the assignment, now is an excellent time. If you have a magnificent speech prepared, I recommend saving it for someone who has finished breakfast.”

Water ticks from a bamboo spout into a stone basin. Three porters cross the practice yard in succession, each carrying the same kind of wrapped load. None of them looks at the narrow opening between the screens.

Yuzuri Kageura is standing beside that opening with a small ornamental gourd in her hand.

“One changed something,” she says. “Nothing stolen. Nothing dangerous. Tell me what you actually saw.”

On the far side of the yard, a young man starts to vault a rail. A voice from the shade tells him the gate was open. He lands badly enough to regret the flourish.

Yuzuri does not turn.

“This is why we practice before accepting money.”

The last porter pauses beside a water channel. A cord hangs from the load; its loose end is a different length from the others. There may be more to notice, or a perfectly ordinary reason for it.

“You can ask a question. You can look again. You can say you don't know. That last one is useful only if it is true.”

She sets the gourd on the rail, giving it a final protective glance. The yard remains open around you, screens stirring in the breeze, with no one yet deciding how you will proceed.
